transcript.text: my belling cooker keeps burnin stuff 1 day then next day its undercookd on same temp. been like it a cuple months. thermastat??

To answer your question directly: while a faulty thermostat can cause temperature issues, 'burning one day and undercooking the next' is rarely just the thermostat. It usually points to uneven heat distribution (the fan) or heat escaping (the door seal). A thermostat fault typically makes the whole oven run consistently too hot or too cold. Here are the two most likely causes:
1. Cavity Fan Motor/Blade: If the fan is slow, noisy, or the blade is loose/bent, heat won't circulate evenly. This often leads to burning on one side and undercooking on the other.
2. Door Seal: If the seal is torn or the door doesn't close flush, heat escapes, causing erratic cooking temperatures. Please check these two things:
1. Open the oven door and look at the fan behind the back panel. Does it spin freely by hand? When you turn the oven on to a normal bake setting (not grill), does it start spinning?
2. Inspect the rubber seal around the inside of the door glass. Is it torn, brittle, or missing any pieces? Let me know what you find with those checks.

ok i can hear the fan going i think, so thats probably spinning every time. didnt try turnin it by hand tho. the door seal is a bit flattened at the top corner but the door shuts ok. i do alot of roasts and lasagne so it matters lol

We need to dig deeper into why the heat distribution is inconsistent. The most likely cause now is that while the fan motor is turning, it might not be circulating air effectively. This happens if the blade is slightly bent, loose on its spindle (so it spins slowly or wobbles), or if the motor itself is wearing out and running too slow to move enough hot air around your roasts and lasagne. 1. With the oven completely cool and switched off at the mains, try to gently wiggle the fan blade by hand (don't force it). Does it feel loose or wobbly on its central spindle?
2. When you turn the oven on, listen closely: does the fan sound like a steady hum, or is there a grinding/rattling noise and does it seem slower than usual? If the blade is loose or the motor sounds strained, that explains the uneven cooking. If it feels tight and sounds normal, we'll look at the temperature sensor next.

havent wiggled the fan blade, not sure i can get at it without takin the back panel off tbh. when its on it just sounds normal to me, no grindin or rattlin, steady noise. what would the temperature sensor thing be?

The temperature sensor is a small metal probe usually located inside the top rear corner of the oven cavity. It tells the cooker how hot it is. On older mechanical Belling cookers, this isn't used; instead, there's a thermostat (often behind the dial or in the side wall). However, whether it's a sensor or a thermostat, erratic temperature control usually points to one of two things: either the heating element at the back isn't getting full power intermittently, or the device measuring the heat is giving wrong readings. Let's check if the element itself is working correctly. Please turn the oven on to Fan Bake (or Conventional) at a standard temperature like 180°C/350°F/Gas Mark 4. Wait about 2-3 minutes. Look through the glass door: does the ring-shaped heating element at the back of the oven glow bright red? Or is it barely warm/dim while the fan spins? If it glows brightly but food still burns/undercooks, we look at the sensor/thermostat. If it doesn't glow or flickers, that's your fault.
hmm im not sure, i cant really tell if its glowing bright or not from looking through the door. what else could i check?

Since you can't easily see if it's glowing through the glass, we need a clearer test. The most likely cause now is that the heating element at the back of the oven is failing intermittently. It might be getting power but not heating up fully, or cutting out and on again, which explains why one day it burns (runs hot) and the next it undercooks (doesn't heat enough). 1. Set the oven to Fan Bake at 180°C/350°F.
2. Wait about 2 minutes for it to warm up.
3. Open the door slightly and look directly at the ring-shaped element at the back of the oven (the one behind the fan).
4. Does it glow bright red all around, or does it stay dark/dim? If it glows brightly but food still cooks unevenly, we'll look at the thermostat next. If it stays dim or doesn't glow at all, that points to a faulty element.
sorry still cant tell if its glowing bright or not, i dont really know what its meant to look like lol. is there anything else i can check without any tools? i dont have a thermometer or anything

Since you can't see the element glow clearly and don't have a thermometer, we need to look at how the oven controls itself. The 'burning one day, undercooking the next' pattern suggests the device that measures or sets the temperature is drifting or failing intermittently. Please tell me: does your cooker use a dial/knob (mechanical) or buttons and a digital screen (electronic)? This tells us whether we are looking at a mechanical thermostat or an electronic sensor, which changes the likely fix.
its knobs, mechanical ones, no screen or buttons. theres little orange light that comes on too. the main oven knob is a bit wobbly as well

The wobbly knob is a very strong clue. On older Belling cookers with mechanical dials, the 'knob' is just plastic that sits on top of the actual thermostat spindle inside the cooker. If the internal thermostat mechanism (the part that clicks and switches the heat on and off) has worn out or lost its calibration, it will switch the heating element on for too long (burning food) and then fail to turn it back on quickly enough when needed (undercooking). The wobbling suggests the spindle is loose or the internal mechanism is slipping. Since you can't easily see inside to check the thermostat itself without an engineer, and the fan/element checks didn't rule this out, this is probably a mechanical thermostat failure. This part requires dismantling the cooker faceplate to access and replace, which involves working near mains connections. Because this involves internal electrical work on a gas/electric appliance (even if just the electric oven side), I recommend calling an engineer to check the main oven thermostat. It is not a safe DIY job for most homeowners due to the risk of electric shock or damaging the gas supply components nearby.

Door seal damage or misalignment (heat escaping unevenly) (medium)
Thermostat or temperature sensor fault (incorrect regulation) (medium)
